  2. 2

    A circle has center (−4,2)(-4, 2)(−4,2) and radius 666. Which equation is its standard form?

    Answer choices for question 2

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Reads the center's coordinates directly from the printed signs instead of flipping them.

    You chose C: Uses the radius itself on the right side instead of its square.

    You chose D: Flips the center's signs and uses the radius instead of its square.

    The distance from the center to any point on the circle is the radius, so square that condition.

    (x−(−4))2+(y−2)2=62  ⟹  (x+4)2+(y−2)2=36.(x-(-4))^2+(y-2)^2=6^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; (x+4)^2+(y-2)^2=36.(x−(−4))2+(y−2)2=62⟹(x+4)2+(y−2)2=36.

    You chose C: Swaps the labels bbb and ccc, reporting the smaller denominator's root as ccc.

    The larger denominator is a2a^2a2. Here 100>36100 > 36100>36 and 100100100 sits under y2y^2y2, so the major axis is vertical.

    a2=100,  b2=36  ⟹  a=10, b=6,c2=a2−b2=100−36=64  ⟹  c=8.a^2=100,\; b^2=36 \;\Longrightarrow\; a=10,\, b=6, \qquad c^2=a^2-b^2=100-36=64 \;\Longrightarrow\; c=8.a2=100,b2=36⟹a=10,b=6,c2=a2−b2=100−36=64⟹c=8.

    A circle has general form x2+y2−10x+2y+13=0x^2+y^2-10x+2y+13=0x2+y2−10x+2y+13=0. What does substituting the point (1,−2)(1,-2)(1,−2) into the left side tell you about its location?

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Computes the correct value but reads a positive result as inside instead of outside.

    You chose B: Makes a sign error while substituting the negative yyy-coordinate.

    You chose D: Omits the y2=(−2)2=4y^2=(-2)^2=4y2=(−2)2=4 term entirely, computing 1−10−4+13=01-10-4+13=01−10−4+13=0.

    Substitute (1,−2)(1,-2)(1,−2) directly into the left side.

    12+(−2)2−10(1)+2(−2)+13=1+4−10−4+13=4.1^2+(-2)^2-10(1)+2(-2)+13=1+4-10-4+13=4.12+(−2)2−10(1)+2(−2)+13=1+4−10−4+13=4.

    A positive value means the point's squared distance from the center exceeds r2r^2r2, so it lies outside.

    Substituting the line y=2x+10y=2x+10y=2x+10 into x2+y2+2x−6y−15=0x^2+y^2+2x-6y-15=0x2+y2+2x−6y−15=0 and simplifying gives x2+6x+5=0x^2+6x+5=0x2+6x+5=0. How many points does the line share with the circle?

    Answer choices for question 9

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Misreads a positive discriminant as negative.

    You chose B: Assumes any quadratic produced by this kind of substitution must have a repeated root.

    You chose C: Thinks a linear substitution can make the equation vanish identically for every xxx.

    Compute the discriminant of x2+6x+5=0x^2+6x+5=0x2+6x+5=0.

    62−4(1)(5)=36−20=16>0.6^2-4(1)(5)=36-20=16>0.62−4(1)(5)=36−20=16>0.

    A positive discriminant means two distinct real roots, so the line is a secant, crossing the circle at two points.

    x2+y2+Dx+Ey+F  =  (x−h)2+(y−k)2−r2.x^2+y^2+Dx+Ey+F \;=\; (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2-r^2.x2+y2+Dx+Ey+F=(x−h)2+(y−k)2−r2.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Find aaa, bbb, and ccc, and note which of the three comes out largest.

      Part B.

    3. C
      Part C.

      A classmate says that since 400>361400>361400>361, this hyperbola must open up and down, quoting the ellipse's rule that the larger denominator names a2a^2a2. Explain specifically why that rule does not apply here, and state the correct test for a hyperbola's orientation.

      Explain why it works A sentence or two. Reasons, not steps. 4 points

    The answer

    Part A

    a=19a=19a=19, b=20b=20b=20, c=761≈27.6c=\sqrt{761}\approx27.6c=761​≈27.6, the largest of the three.

    Part B

    Vertices (±19,0)(\pm19,0)(±19,0); foci (±761,0)(\pm\sqrt{761},0)(±761​,0); asymptotes y=±2019xy=\pm\dfrac{20}{19}xy=±1920​x.

    Part C

    A hyperbola's orientation is decided by which term is POSITIVE, not which denominator is larger; here x2x^2x2 is positive even though its denominator (361361361) is smaller than y2y^2y2's (400400400), so the branches open left and right despite 400>361400>361400>361.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The x2x^2x2 term is positive, so a2=361a^2=361a2=361 and b2=400b^2=400b2=400.

    a=19,b=20,c2=a2+b2=361+400=761  ⟹  c=761≈27.6.a=19, \quad b=20, \qquad c^2=a^2+b^2=361+400=761 \;\Longrightarrow\; c=\sqrt{761}\approx27.6.a=19,b=20,c2=a2+b2=361+400=761⟹c=761​≈27.6.

    Since c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2 adds two positive numbers, ccc is always the largest of the three for a hyperbola.

    Part B

    Vertices and foci lie on the transverse (horizontal) axis, aaa and ccc from the center: (±19,0)(\pm19,0)(±19,0) and (±761,0)(\pm\sqrt{761},0)(±761​,0).

    The asymptote slope is ±ba\pm\frac{b}{a}±ab​ when x2x^2x2 is positive.

    y=±2019x.y=\pm\frac{20}{19}x.y=±1920​x.

    Part C

    The ellipse's rule (larger denominator names a2a^2a2, and the major axis follows it) comes from the requirement a≥ba \ge ba≥b built into a2=b2+c2a^2=b^2+c^2a2=b2+c2, which forces a2a^2a2 to be the larger of the two ellipse denominators every time.

    A hyperbola has no such requirement: its relation is c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2, with aaa and bbb unconstrained relative to each other, so a2a^2a2 can sit under either the larger OR the smaller denominator.

    x2361−y2400=1  ⟹  x2 positive, though 361<400  ⟹  opens left and right.\frac{x^2}{361}-\frac{y^2}{400}=1 \;\Longrightarrow\; x^2 \text{ positive, though } 361<400 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{opens left and right.}361x2​−400y2​=1⟹x2 positive, though 361<400⟹opens left and right.

    What fixes a2a^2a2's position is which term carries a PLUS sign, since aaa is always measured along the transverse axis, the axis the curve actually crosses. The classmate's rule, borrowed from the wrong curve, gives the wrong answer.

The branches open left and right because x2x^2x2 is the positive term, even though its denominator 361361361 is smaller than 400400400: a hyperbola's orientation follows the sign of the term, not the size of the denominator, unlike an ellipse.

      Part C.

      Explain why multiplying every term of a general-form equation by a positive constant (as the original equation does, with 444) never changes which points are classified as inside, on, or outside, even though it changes every coefficient DDD, EEE, and FFF.

    The answer

    Part A

    It is a circle: (x−1)2+(y+5)2=25(x-1)^2+(y+5)^2=25(x−1)2+(y+5)2=25.

    Part B

    404040, positive, so (2,3)(2,3)(2,3) is outside the circle.

    Part C

    Multiplying the whole expression by a positive constant multiplies its value at every point by that same positive constant, which cannot change the value's sign, and the inside/on/outside classification depends only on that sign.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The coefficients on x2x^2x2 and y2y^2y2 are equal and share a sign (444 and 444), which is the circle case. Divide by 444 and complete the square.

    x2+y2−2x+10y+1=0  ⟹  (x−1)2+(y+5)2=−1+1+25=25.x^2+y^2-2x+10y+1=0 \;\Longrightarrow\; (x-1)^2+(y+5)^2=-1+1+25=25.x2+y2−2x+10y+1=0⟹(x−1)2+(y+5)2=−1+1+25=25.

    Part B

    22+32−2(2)+10(3)+1=4+9−4+30+1=40.2^2+3^2-2(2)+10(3)+1=4+9-4+30+1=40.22+32−2(2)+10(3)+1=4+9−4+30+1=40.

    Positive, so the point lies outside the circle.

    Part C

    Let g(x,y)=x2+y2+Dx+Ey+Fg(x,y)=x^2+y^2+Dx+Ey+Fg(x,y)=x2+y2+Dx+Ey+F be the reduced expression and k>0k>0k>0 a positive constant. The scaled equation is k⋅g(x,y)=0k \cdot g(x,y)=0k⋅g(x,y)=0, and at any point (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) its left side is exactly k⋅g(x,y)k \cdot g(x,y)k⋅g(x,y).

    sign⁡(k⋅g(x,y))=sign⁡(g(x,y))for every k>0.\operatorname{sign}\bigl(k \cdot g(x,y)\bigr) = \operatorname{sign}\bigl(g(x,y)\bigr) \quad \text{for every } k>0.sign(k⋅g(x,y))=sign(g(x,y))for every k>0.

    Multiplying a real number by a positive constant can change its size but never its sign. Since the location test reads only the SIGN of the expression at a point, scaling the whole equation by a positive constant leaves every classification unchanged, even though DDD, EEE, and FFF themselves are multiplied by kkk and look different.

    In one line

    4x2+4y2−8x+40y+4=04x^2+4y^2-8x+40y+4=04x2+4y2−8x+40y+4=0 is a circle, (x−1)2+(y+5)2=25(x-1)^2+(y+5)^2=25(x−1)2+(y+5)2=25; the point (2,3)(2,3)(2,3) gives 404040 in the reduced general form, so it lies outside. Scaling a general-form equation by a positive constant multiplies the expression's value at every point by that same constant, which cannot flip its sign, so the inside/on/outside classification never changes even though DDD, EEE, FFF do.

    Part A

    a=6a=6a=6, b=25b=2\sqrt{5}b=25​, c=4c=4c=4. Vertices (±6,0)(\pm6,0)(±6,0), foci (±4,0)(\pm4,0)(±4,0).

    Part B

    14x2−90x+45=014x^2-90x+45=014x2−90x+45=0; discriminant 558055805580, positive, so the line meets the ellipse at two points.

    Part C

    The SIGN of b2−4acb^2-4acb2−4ac alone decides whether the roots are real and distinct, real and repeated, or complex, before any square root is taken. Its SQUARE-STATUS is a separate question, deciding only whether real roots are rational or irrational, and that second question needs aaa, bbb, ccc themselves to be rational.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The larger denominator, 363636, sits under x2x^2x2: a2=36a^2=36a2=36, b2=20b^2=20b2=20, so a=6a=6a=6, b=20=25b=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5b=20​=25​.

    Multiply by 180180180, the least common multiple of 363636 and 202020, to clear both fractions at once.

    (−90)2−4(14)(45)=8100−2520=5580>0.(-90)^2-4(14)(45)=8100-2520=5580>0.(−90)2−4(14)(45)=8100−2520=5580>0.

    Positive, so the line is a secant, meeting the ellipse at two points.

    Part C

    The quadratic formula's classification of roots, two real, one repeated, or a complex pair, rests entirely on the SIGN of b2−4acb^2-4acb2−4ac, decided before any square root is ever taken. A positive value of any size guarantees two distinct real roots by that sign test alone.

    5580>0  ⟹  two distinct real roots.5580>0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{two distinct real roots}.5580>0⟹two distinct real roots.

    Whether that positive value is a perfect square is a separate question, controlling only whether b2−4ac\sqrt{b^2-4ac}b2−4ac​ itself comes out rational (giving rational roots) or irrational (giving roots that are real but not expressible as simple fractions). This second question needs aaa, bbb, ccc to be rational numbers in the first place, since "rational versus irrational" is not even the right pair of options for roots built from irrational coefficients.

    5580 is a positive integer, not a perfect square  ⟹  5580∉Q  ⟹  the two roots are irrational.5580 \text{ is a positive integer, not a perfect square} \;\Longrightarrow\; \sqrt{5580} \notin \mathbb{Q} \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{the two roots are irrational.}5580 is a positive integer, not a perfect square⟹5580​∈/Q⟹the two roots are irrational.

    But the two intersection points are still exactly two, and still exactly real, because that verdict was already settled by the sign of 558055805580 alone, before its square root was ever considered. For any quadratic with RATIONAL coefficients, however messy, the sign test and the perfect-square test remain two different questions.

    In one line

    a=6a=6a=6, b=25b=2\sqrt{5}b=25​, c=4c=4c=4, vertices (±6,0)(\pm6,0)(±6,0), foci (±4,0)(\pm4,0)(±4,0). The line y=x−5y=x-5y=x−5 substituted into the ellipse gives 14x2−90x+45=014x^2-90x+45=014x2−90x+45=0, discriminant 5580>05580>05580>0, so the line is a secant meeting the ellipse at two points. That the discriminant is a positive, non-square integer only means the two points have irrational coordinates; the sign of the discriminant alone, decided before any square root, already guarantees they are real and distinct.

      Model the situation Name your unknown first, then write every other quantity in terms of that one letter. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      A support strut attaches to the dish at the point where x=12x=12x=12 cm from the vertex line. How far above the vertex does the strut attach, and how far is that point from the focus?

      Carry your own answer forward Use your own equation from part A.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Explain, using the definition of a parabola (not the shortcut formula), why the strut's distance to the focus found in part B must equal its distance to the directrix, and state the directrix's equation.

      Carry your own answer forward Use your own ppp and the strut's height from parts A and B.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 4 points

    The answer

    Part A

    x2=72yx^2=72yx2=72y.

    Part B

    y=2y=2y=2 cm above the vertex; focal distance 202020 cm.

    Part C

    By definition, every point of a parabola is equidistant from the focus and the directrix, so the strut's focal distance, 202020 cm, must equal its distance to the directrix y=−18y=-18y=−18; checking directly, the strut sits at height y=2y=2y=2, which is 2−(−18)=202-(-18)=202−(−18)=20 cm above that line, confirming it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The vertex is at the origin and the focal length is p=18p=18p=18, with the parabola opening upward, so it takes the form x2=4pyx^2=4pyx2=4py.

    x2=4(18)y=72y.x^2=4(18)y=72y.x2=4(18)y=72y.

    Part B

    Substitute x=12x=12x=12.

    122=72y  ⟹  144=72y  ⟹  y=2.12^2=72y \;\Longrightarrow\; 144=72y \;\Longrightarrow\; y=2.122=72y⟹144=72y⟹y=2.

    The focus is (0,18)(0,18)(0,18). The shortcut PF=y+pPF=y+pPF=y+p gives

    PF=2+18=20 cm,PF=2+18=20 \text{ cm},PF=2+18=20 cm,

    and the distance formula agrees: (12−0)2+(2−18)2=144+256=400=20\sqrt{(12-0)^2+(2-18)^2}=\sqrt{144+256}=\sqrt{400}=20(12−0)2+(2−18)2​=144+256​=400​=20 cm.

    Part C

    A parabola is DEFINED as the set of points equidistant from a focus and a directrix; the shortcut PF=y+pPF=y+pPF=y+p is not an extra fact layered on top of that definition, it is exactly what the distance to the directrix simplifies to for a point above a directrix at y=−py=-py=−p.

    The directrix here is y=−p=−18y=-p=-18y=−p=−18. The strut sits at (12,2)(12,2)(12,2), so its distance to the directrix is

    2−(−18)=20 cm,2-(-18)=20 \text{ cm},2−(−18)=20 cm,

    exactly matching the focal distance of 202020 cm found in part B by the shortcut. The two distances agree not by coincidence but because the shortcut IS the directrix-distance computation, restated, and the defining condition of the parabola sets that equal to the focal distance for every point of the curve.

    In one line

    x2=72yx^2=72yx2=72y; the strut attaches at (12,2)(12,2)(12,2), 222 cm above the vertex, and 202020 cm from the focus. Its distance to the directrix y=−18y=-18y=−18 is also 2−(−18)=202-(-18)=202−(−18)=20 cm, matching exactly, because the shortcut PF=y+pPF=y+pPF=y+p is the directrix-distance side of the parabola's own defining condition, not a separate fact.

  10. 10

    10. Two relations that point opposite ways . 12 points. This question goes beyond core Algebra II. It is not required by the course. Question 10 of 10.

    12 pts Advanced. This question goes beyond core Algebra II. It is not required by the course.

    An ellipse and a hyperbola obey opposite relations: c2=a2−b2c^2=a^2-b^2c2=a2−b2 for the ellipse, c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2 for the hyperbola.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Consider a general ellipse centered at the origin with foci (±c,0)(\pm c,0)(±c,0) and semi-minor axis bbb, so its co-vertex is (0,b)(0,b)(0,b). Using only the fact that the co-vertex is equidistant from both foci, and that the sum of its two focal distances is 2a2a2a, show that each focal distance from the co-vertex equals aaa exactly, and hence that a2=b2+c2a^2=b^2+c^2a2=b2+c2.

      Complete the derivation Each line should follow from the one above it. Say what lets you take each step. 4 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Now take as GIVEN that a general hyperbola centered at the origin with foci (±c,0)(\pm c,0)(±c,0), vertices (±a,0)(\pm a,0)(±a,0), and conjugate semi-axis bbb satisfies c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2 (established, as in this chapter, from the hyperbola's own difference-of-distances condition). Using that given relation, verify that the central rectangle's corner (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) (the rectangle reaching aaa along the transverse axis and bbb along the conjugate axis) sits exactly a distance ccc from the center.

      Complete the derivation Each line should follow from the one above it. Say what lets you take each step. 3 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Part A derived a2=b2+c2a^2=b^2+c^2a2=b2+c2 from a genuine POINT ON THE ELLIPSE, the co-vertex, using the curve's own sum condition. Part B, by contrast, had to take c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2 as GIVEN before verifying a fact about the rectangle's corner. Explain specifically why the corner cannot be used the way Part A used the co-vertex, that is, why no argument starting from a curve point's own defining condition was available to derive the relation from the corner directly.

      Carry your own answer forward Refer to your own proofs from parts A and B.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    Since the co-vertex (0,b)(0,b)(0,b) is equidistant from both foci and its two focal distances sum to 2a2a2a, each distance is aaa; computing that distance directly gives b2+c2=a\sqrt{b^2+c^2}=ab2+c2​=a, so a2=b2+c2a^2=b^2+c^2a2=b2+c2.

    Part B

    The distance from the origin to the corner (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) is a2+b2\sqrt{a^2+b^2}a2+b2​ by the Pythagorean theorem, and since c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2 is given, that distance equals c2=c\sqrt{c^2}=cc2​=c exactly.

    Part C

    The corner is not a point on the hyperbola, so the curve's own difference condition cannot apply to it as the sum condition applied to the ellipse's co-vertex; the corner is well-defined only once aaa, bbb, ccc are already known, so Part B verifies the relation rather than deriving it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The co-vertex (0,b)(0,b)(0,b) sits on the yyy-axis, which is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining (±c,0)(\pm c,0)(±c,0), so it is equidistant from both foci. Call that common distance ddd. Since the SUM of the two focal distances is always 2a2a2a on an ellipse, and both distances equal ddd here,

    d+d=2a  ⟹  d=a.d+d=2a \;\Longrightarrow\; d=a.d+d=2a⟹d=a.

    Now compute ddd directly, using the distance formula from (0,b)(0,b)(0,b) to (c,0)(c,0)(c,0):

    d=(c−0)2+(0−b)2=c2+b2.d=\sqrt{(c-0)^2+(0-b)^2}=\sqrt{c^2+b^2}.d=(c−0)2+(0−b)2​=c2+b2​.

    Setting the two expressions for ddd equal:

    b2+c2=a  ⟹  a2=b2+c2.\sqrt{b^2+c^2}=a \;\Longrightarrow\; a^2=b^2+c^2.b2+c2​=a⟹a2=b2+c2.

    Part B

    The distance from the center (the origin) to the corner (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) is, by the Pythagorean theorem,

    (a−0)2+(b−0)2=a2+b2.\sqrt{(a-0)^2+(b-0)^2}=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.(a−0)2+(b−0)2​=a2+b2​.

    Since c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2 is given, a2+b2=c2=c\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=\sqrt{c^2}=ca2+b2​=c2​=c. So the corner-to-center distance is exactly ccc: the central rectangle's half-diagonal matches the focal distance, which is why the rectangle is a useful picture for the hyperbola's three lengths, not a source of the relation itself.

    Part C

    Part A's argument works because the co-vertex is a genuine point ON THE ELLIPSE, so the curve's own defining sum condition applies to it directly, the same way it applies to every other point of the curve.

    co-vertex on curve  ⟹  PF1+PF2=2a applies to it directly.\text{co-vertex on curve} \;\Longrightarrow\; PF_1+PF_2=2a \text{ applies to it directly.}co-vertex on curve⟹PF1​+PF2​=2a applies to it directly.

    The central rectangle's corner in part B is not a point on the hyperbola at all. It is an auxiliary construction whose coordinates ARE aaa and bbb, so asking a curve point's defining condition (the difference ∣PF1−PF2∣=2a|PF_1-PF_2|=2a∣PF1​−PF2​∣=2a) to say something about it does not even make sense: the corner has no pair of focal distances to take a difference of, because it never claims to lie on the curve. The only way to know the corner sits a distance ccc from the center is to already know c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2, which is exactly what Part B assumed as given.

    That is why c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2 genuinely needs to be established the way the ellipse's relation was in Part A: starting from the hyperbola's own difference condition at a real point of the curve (for instance a vertex, or a general point, followed by clearing the two radicals by squaring twice), the way the lesson derives the standard-form equation. Part B's rectangle argument, once that relation is available, is a useful geometric PICTURE of it, not a second independent route to it.

    In one line

    For an ellipse, the co-vertex is equidistant from both foci and its two focal distances sum to 2a2a2a, so each equals aaa; computing that distance directly gives a2=b2+c2a^2=b^2+c^2a2=b2+c2, i.e. c2=a2−b2c^2=a^2-b^2c2=a2−b2, a genuine derivation from a curve point. For a hyperbola, GIVEN c2=a2+b2c^2=a^2+b^2c2=a2+b2, the central rectangle's corner (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) checks out as exactly ccc from the center by the Pythagorean theorem, but this is a verification, not a derivation: the corner is not a point on the hyperbola, so the curve's own difference condition cannot be applied to it the way the sum condition was applied to the ellipse's co-vertex. The relation itself is established the same way the ellipse's was, from the difference condition at a genuine curve point.
